#9059. Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Photography by Peter Vinther (unless stated otherwise)

Architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it’s rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck, Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster, Ryom showed her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020, and Ukurant quickly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen’s master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom’s tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair, made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

“I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a new logic through simple gestures,” Urquiola said of why she chose Ryom.

“There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself.

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

“During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I’m kind of doing – I don’t see myself as limited to one material,” Ryom told Dezeen.

While she “really strongly identifies as a furniture designer”, Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

“Even when I’m doing collectible things for galleries, I’m always thinking of the functionality of the pieces,” she explained.

“Even if you can say, ‘[what’s functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair’, as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that’s still a function or a means to an end.”

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

“I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing,” Ryom explained.

“That’s something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.”

The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom’s pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

“Even if people don’t think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it’s completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition,” she explained.

“I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it].”

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of big brands, such as IKEA and Disney, working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn’t always aware of the people behind the products.

“I think it’s an important thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation,” Ryom said.

“Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they’re still trying to figure out ‘what is it that you actually do’?

Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it

Ryom herself, meanwhile, says she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from “starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft”.

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

“Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it,” she said.

“Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is.”

As someone who’s constantly exploring new materials and ways of designing, Ryom also highlights the importance of collaboration. She says that while she likes doing a lot of the work on her furniture herself, she has also gotten better at reaching out to experts to get input for some of her pieces, including her Enfold chair.

The steel chair is covered in a ruched leather upholstery, held in place by buttons, that creates a very tactile, sculptural seat.

“It did it all myself, but I reached out to a fashion designer who does a lot of leather bags, and I could talk to her and ask ‘how would you do the finishing here, or what kind of tool would you use there?'” she said.“I really like figuring things out myself and doing it myself, but seeking the knowledge of those people who have really done the craft.”

Being chosen by Urquiola meant a lot to Ryom, who really admires the Spanish designer.

“It was actually a little surreal, because she is someone that I look up to,” Ryom said. “When you can say anyone in the world, I feel very, very honoured that she pointed at me – that’s a huge thing.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#9057. Comment | Cop31 may have faltered but, as grassroots initiatives in the art world and beyond remind us‚ all is not lost

This year's United Nations Climate Change Conference, known as Cop31, concluded with no deal on Sunday, 22 November, two days after it was set to close

In this monthly column, Louisa Buck looks at how the art world is responding to the environmental and climate crisis.

The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern. Despite the talks in Antalya, Turkey running over by two days as delegates struggled to achieve a consensus, they were ultimately derailed by the refusal by a group of oil producing states—led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia—to allow any mention of fossil fuel in the conference’s final agreement. This despite an agreement already made at Cop28 in 2023 to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas. As a result, more than 130 countries, including the European Union (EU) and the UK, refused to sign off a deal which omitted any reference to the main cause of climate change.

“We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”

Much of the art on display at Cop also seemed out of kilter with the urgency of the times. The centrepiece of the official CopArt programme, which was installed across the Cop site and curated by art advisor and contemporary art curator Nagihan Ozel, was an extensive installation of 18 mirror panels installed in the Green Zone and created by veteran artist Heinz Mack who has been making similar work since the 1960s. Other conspicuous pieces included Anselm Kiefer’s giant seascape bearing a pair of metal scales, Für Rabbi Löw (2010-12) and a forest made from recycled cardboard from Eva Jospin. Two monumental bronze sculptures by Belgian artist Koen Vanmechelen, one of an ape standing on a mirrored glass sphere balanced on a human thumb and another of a child struggling to hold an iguana, are described by the artist as “exploring our relationship with the natural world.”

Also on show in the Cop Green Zone and an especially jarring symbol of the deep schisms and incompatible agendas that characterised this latest Conference of the Parties were five animal sculptures created from discarded electronic and industrial defence waste materials. These were part of the “Upcycling a Future Vision” art collection launched by Aselsan, Turkey’s largest defence contractor to demonstrate its “commitment to a circular economy”, according to Turkish state-run media, as well as to celebrate the company’s 50th anniversary and “future of more efficient, innovative and sustainable production.” In a further irony, the defence giant—which is majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation and produces electronic warfare technology and naval and air defence missile systems—was awarded a Green Transformation certificate from the Turkish authorities in tribute to its sustainability efforts. These apparently include a five-year road map to maximise energy, water and raw material efficiency whilst reducing carbon emissions and recycling 87% of total waste.

But amidst the chaos and anomalies within Cop some consolation can be gleaned from the fact that, while the oil-producing countries united to derail proceedings (undoubtedly spurred by the absence of an official US delegation and the Trump administration's overt hostility to the global fight to combat climate change), nonetheless 193 countries plus the EU remain committed to the Paris Agreement. Collectively these nations account for around 85% of global emissions. And while not wrapped up in a final deal, a number of significant agreements were made at Cop31 which included countries backing faster electrification and clean energy, drawing up measures to cut methane emissions and passing measures to protect the planet’s forests and oceans and strengthen support for communities impacted by climate change.

Beyond the Cop negotiating rooms, there are also glimmers of progress. In the UK greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by more than 50% since 1990 (although this much-vaunted statistic doesn’t include international aviation, shipping and imports and exports, which makes it more like 24%, according to the Office for National Statistics). Solar panels now provide 28% of Pakistan’s power while France and Denmark have announced roadmaps to phase out all fossil fuel by 2050, with Spain, Portugal and other countries planning to do the same. While these shifts often have as much to do with the fall in the cost of renewable technology and its resilience to market swings as a desire to hit climate goals; nonetheless an incremental frustration at the Cop consensus model means that countries are increasingly going it alone in naming what needs to be done and in identifying how they will tackle it.

Still from The People's Emergency Briefing (2026) featuring naturalist and presenter Chris Packham

Case in point was last Monday (16 November) when, as Cop31 was rumbling on, an important milestone was reached in the UK as Parliament debated a nearly 139,000 strong petition which called for the government to hold a UK-wide emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. The petition had been generated by the National Emergency Briefing (NEB), a public information campaign consisting of an influential group of leading experts and fronted by the British naturalist and BBC TV presenter Chris Packham. It was asking for a “prime-time Covid-style briefing across all channels” which would be introduced by the Prime Minister and delivered by independent experts in order to spell out the extent and risks posed by climate change and nature loss, along with the action—both public and governmental—that needs to be taken. More than seventy members of parliament from across the political spectrum attended the three-hour debate which ended broadly in favour of the proposed televised emergency briefing, although not officially agreed. Speaking for the government, climate transition minister Katie White MP did go on record to state that she and her colleagues would meet with the leaders of the NEB campaign and “explore opportunities to work together”, and work on public engagement within the government's climate and nature security taskforce.

Just as Westminster was being galvanised by the NEB campaign, so too was the art world. Two days after the briefing debate, Tate Modern hosted a packed screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing, a 50-minute documentary film made by the NEB and presented by Packham. An articulate panel of nine experts starkly presented the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, nature, the economy, national security and public health. This film, which anyone can freely register to screen, has been responsible for fueling much of the groundswell of both public and parliamentary support for the NEB’s petition. Since its release in April last year, The People’s Emergency Briefing has been shown more than 5000 times across myriad sectors and in venues large and small throughout the UK, from church halls, offices and hospitals, with many more scheduled for the forthcoming months. As Katie White declared at the Parliamentary debate, “a film has become a movement.”

However—with a few notable exceptions—the People’s Emergency Briefing has not had much airing in the art world. But now this seems set to change thanks to the art world environmental charity the Gallery Climate Coalition (GCC), who organised the screening and the following panel discussion. This was chaired by Frances Morris, the former director of Tate Modern and nowthe GCC's chair, speaking with artist Heather Ackroyd and Peter Lefort, the green futures network manager at the University of Exeter.

The screening of The People's Emergency Briefing at Tate Modern on 18 November 2026

Among the two-hundred strong audience of artists, including Cornelia Parker and Marcus Coates, academics and art workers from across both the public and commercial sectors, there emerged a strong determination to galvanise action. Many declared a commitment to lobby their MPs, to organise screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing in their galleries and generally to be more courageous in both acting individually and collectively to help instigate what Peter Lefort compellingly described as “positive tipping points.”

As Lefort explained, these tipping points occur when cumulative changes in behaviour, policies, expectations and attitudes reinforce each other and gather momentum to accelerate change and achieve transformative impact. As politicians falter and our systems for joining forces globally become increasingly dysfunctional and inflexible, it now seems increasingly clear that these new forces for change—such as the NEB, with allied activist groups and screenings occuring across Europe—are coming from the grassroots up, and that the creativity of the art world needs to be applied to shift ossified, seemingly intractable structures and open up new ways of thinking.

After all, it was back in 2019 that, on the instigation of artist duo Heather Ackroyd and Dan Harvey, a procession of bell ringing artworkers headed by a woman wearing a coat of living grass and riding a white horse, occupied Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. The event from the Culture Declares Emergency movement inspired then-director Frances Morris to make the institution of Tate declare a climate and ecological emergency, helping set in motion an increased environmental awareness that is now common currency throughout the art world. In the words of one attendee at last week’s Tate Modern gathering, “we may be small compared to other sectors but we can be LOUD!” So now let’s brush ourselves down after Cop and make our voices heard, before it is too late.

#9056. Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

It is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday! While our Film Fridays tend to spotlight a single emulsion, with this annual celebration we feature the entire selection of black and white film stocks that we have in our inventory. But before we dig in too far, it would be a good moment to explain our inspiration for Film Friday.

This story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR. Blue Moon offers film, development services, printing, and even an ever-rotating line of film cameras and lenses.

PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!

Blue Moon Camera and Machine launched Film Friday publicly in 2019, but it had been an ongoing project of ours for several years prior to that. The film that started it all was Ilford XP2. See, we (the collective “we”, that is, as in all of us film photographers) have always had an amazing selection of films to choose from as we decide what to load in our cameras. This selection has evolved over time. Some years it has winnowed down, and other years it has actually expanded. But there have always been just so many films out there to make our work and art with. It is also true, however, that most of us gravitate to certain films. We find the emulsion we like, and we settle into it.

This is neither a good behavior nor a bad one—perhaps it is both; it is simply what we tend to do. And even when you work in an all-analog camera store, like Blue Moon Camera, you can fall into these patterns. And this is where XP2 comes in. Ilford XP2 was one of those films we never used all that much. To be honest, Kodak Tri-X and Ilford HP5 were our typical go-to film stocks. Yet every now and then we would find cause to shoot with a roll of XP2 instead.

This might happen two or three times a year. And each of those times we would get the negatives back and think to ourselves, “Wow, XP2 is a gorgeous film. Why don’t we use this stuff more often?” Of course, the answer is because we know what we know, and we like to stick with that. And thus we decided to set about changing this. We made it a personal project to not just shoot a roll of every film we carried, but actually use it repeatedly and get to know it. One film at a time we would go out for several months, working through multiple rolls, taking our time, learning each emulsion’s quirks and characteristics, and then coalescing those experiences into a collection of images and a written review. The goal was to pass along not just the knowledge and experience we had gained, but the inspiration as well.

There is something to be said for working in depth and committing to a single film and knowing it like you know nothing else. But there is also something to be said about breadth and being familiar with all the myriad options open to you in your creative pursuits. And that is the beating heart of our Film Fridays. It is about celebrating the wealth of options open to us. It is about reminding ourselves that there are more films out there than simply Ultramax, Portra, or HP5. And of course, it is about learning and growing as film photographers.

So having said all that, we came up with the idea of Black (and White) Film Friday only a few years ago. Yes, it is timed to coincide with Black Friday, and yes, quite admittedly, there is a bit of a commercial gimmick built into that. But there is also more to our B&W Film Friday than the sales angle. Let us explain.

In a similar way to how many of us gravitate toward a select few film stocks, we have also noticed that, generally speaking, many film photographers lean toward color film photography. This is especially true with newer film photographers. A big reason is we see the world, and our lives, in color, so it is a natural or even reflexive deduction to photograph with color film. Time and again we have had customers at the counter ask for film recommendations, and we, in turn, ask if they are interested in color or B&W film. It is not uncommon for them to respond to that simple question with some surprise that they had not even considered black and white and had never even tried a roll of it. This is the thing with habits; they tend to fit so snugly we can forget they are even there.

But B&W film should not be forgotten or overlooked. In short, there is a classic beauty and a timelessness that can only be captured with B&W film. It also simplifies the world in its way by converting colors that may otherwise be distracting into tones of grey and letting us make images about something other than the reds, oranges, yellows, greens, blues, and violets of the world.

Black and white allows us to focus on light, textures, relationships, shapes, patterns, grit, grain, and so many other elements (or ideas). It isn’t that you cannot do these things with color film—you can—but there is a directness with which B&W lets you approach these things. This is harder to understand via explanation than it is through experience. So we run our B&W Film Friday not just for the photographers who already love their black and white films, but also for those who have never stepped into those waters.

And there is a crazy variety out there to work with. There are more different types of black and white films than there are color films. We did a rough count, and once you eliminate all the different format choices and focus on just the different emulsions, we have at least 45 unique film stocks to try.

These films are mostly of the black and white negative type, but there are a few reversal films as well and also a couple of black and white instant films to keep in mind. Let’s repeat that number for emphasis: there are at least 45 unique black and white films in our inventory alone. And we don’t even carry every possible B&W film option on the market. That is easily in the 50s and maybe the 60s once you go out into the wider market looking for these films.

So what are you waiting for? That is a lot of film to try, and our guess is most of you have perhaps not even used half of these. So take advantage of this one day where you can pick up more of your favorite B&W film, or you can try something entirely new. We heartily recommend doing both. Visit our online store or come by our shop in St. Johns, Portland, Oregon, and get some film.

If you're looking for a handheld console that ISN'T a Nintendo Switch 2 this Black Friday, then I've got the perfect deal for you. I love my Switch 2, but after testing out the new Acer Predator Atlas 8 for the last few days, I'm 100% a convert. It's £235 off over at Very in the UK right now, which is a steal price for anyone looking for a Switch alternative to PC gaming on the go.

The Black Friday deal I've found is on the model I currently have, and the cheapest configuration. You get a 120 Hz refresh rate, Intel Arc G3 processor, 16GB of RAM and 512GB of SSD storage, plus a gorgeous 8-inch display and Windows 11 installed.

The best part? You can bag an extra 10% off today when shopping with Very using the code BFSAVE, which brings the final price down from £999.99 RRP to just £764.10 (10% off £849) – a £235 saving!! We're not done yet either – gamers who buy the console and register their purchase via the Acer UK Offers portal can claim £265 in free loot/accessories and get a free copy of the mountain-biking title Mavrix, too.

I can honestly say, from the few weeks I've had with it, that my gaming experience feels so premium. Pair this with the Chizha Mount Ling 2 Pro Smart Creator Dock, and you're basically a pro gamer.

Freebies up for grabs from Acer include a Gaming Dock, 100W GaN Fast Charger, and a 3-Year Extended Warranty. Extreme-edition models also score an NVMe SSD Enclosure, Predator Wireless Controller, and a free digital copy of the mountain-biking title Mavrix.

There are several big advantages of a handheld PC over a beefy gaming PC, as well as in comparison with more family-friendly consoles like the Nintendo Switch 2.

Despite what my headline says, it isn't necessarily about which of these consoles is the "best", as they're catered to 2 entirely different demographics.

I had never considered a handheld PC prior to getting the Atlas, given that I'm more of a cosy gamer. Animal Crossing, Pokopia, and Disney Dreamlight Valley have always been my comfort games, but knowing that I can play juicier titles like Jurassic World Evolution 3, Marvel Rivals, and even a bit of Death Stranding from the comfort of my sofa if I fancy is a luxury you can't put a price on.

I've had my PlayStation 5 for what feels like a decade now, but it's become something of a paperweight recently since my desk has been overtaken by work priorities and filming gear. While I did consider the PlayStation Portal, the reviews weren't really selling it for me.

Having a powerful handheld PC that I can pick up and move with me on the go means clutter doesn't limit my gaming time anymore. I can pick it up and put it down whenever without relying on a large monitor or being tied to a chair.

For portability, comfort, power, performance, and ease of use (no building your own PC from scratch), this console is five stars and worth every penny in my opinion. Sure, you can get rivals like the ASUS ROG Ally or Lenovo Legion Go for a lot less, but the Intel Arc G3 processor alone is revolutionary and currently the strongest PC gaming handheld silicon available.

#9054. Wine bar informs rich colour palette for Yorkshire home renovation by Tuckey Design Studio

London architecture practice Tuckey Design Studio has renovated and extended Bay House in rural Yorkshire, using a rich, moody palette intended to evoke the feeling of a wine bar.

The project involved reconfiguring and expanding the country house dating from the early 2000s, while introducing a garden spa and sauna.

Tuckey Design Studio was tasked by the clients to recreate the feeling of their favourite wine bar, which informed a palette of dark timber carpentry, terracotta-painted walls and a bespoke wine storage cabinet alongside a tasting area.

“The ambition was clear from the beginning: to bring the atmosphere of a much-loved London wine bar into the home,” project lead Fraser Biggins told Dezeen.

“The clients’ enthusiasm for wine and music became important touchstones for the design, informing both the arrangement of the spaces and the character of the interiors,” he added.

The home’s previously cramped interiors are now centred on a large, double-height atrium, which serves as both a point of arrival and a gathering and tasting space with a bespoke timber “wine wall”.

This hall is finished with dark timber panelling, terrazzo floors and terracotta paintwork, with a wall alongside an arched composite stone staircase punctured by small square openings.

This central space leads through into the social spaces, with a kitchen and dining space finished using similar dark timber panelling and concrete countertops.

The stairs lead up to the first floor via a landing with a built-in bench, where a balcony connecting the bedrooms enjoys views of the hall below. It also looks across the garden through windows in a new bay window extension.

“The central hall forms the organising principle of the house, providing a shared space from which the surrounding family rooms and activities unfold,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“A series of interconnected spaces, galleries and overlooking balconies create visual connections across different levels, allowing the house to feel both connected and varied,” he added.

On the first floor, two of the existing bedrooms have been converted into a games room and bar space, finished in dark shades of green and grey.

Alongside them are four ensuite bedrooms finished in warmer shades of pale pink and yellow, with each featuring a hand-painted mural designed to “reflect the character of each occupant”.

“Material choices were guided by a desire for honesty, durability and longevity,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“We wanted the spaces to feel timeless and comfortable, without relying too heavily on traditional materials or references.”

“Instead, the palette brings together robust, tactile finishes that feel natural and lived-in, allowing the character of the materials to speak for themselves,” he added.

The exterior of the extension has been finished in composite stone and dark accoya wood, and looks across the home’s garden to the standalone spa and sauna, which was designed as a “complementary counterpoint” to the main home.

Previous projects by Tuckey Design Studio include a home in Wiltshire constructed using walls of unstabilised rammed earth and a residence within a converted chapel in Devon.

#9052. Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study says

The director of the Australian Museum, Kim McKay, and Koro Johnny Tuki, representing the Rapa Nui people, mark the handing over of remains of Indigenous people in July Photo: Louise Reily; © Australian Museum

Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the issue.

“Argentina is central to any discussion of this issue in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”

The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.

Those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and said: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”

According to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she says, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.

“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala says, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”

Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.

A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, shows how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.

“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, says the return of the child from Apu Chañi shows that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.

That, she says, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.

At the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.

For Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she says. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.

Reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.

Pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she says. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.

In Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she says, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”

The restituted human remains include 17 skulls and one sample of hair, which were taken from the island during a German expedition in 1882

On public view for the first time, the objects were all returned during outgoing president Gustavo Petro’s administration

The institution intensified its repatriation efforts after revised federal rules governing Native American remains and funerary objects went into effect earlier this year

#9050. Even if the Nikon D850 Is Discontinued, It Won’t Be Hard To Buy

Even if the Nikon D850 Is Discontinued, It Won’t Be Hard To Buy

The Nikon D850 may be on its last legs, but that doesn’t mean photographers can no longer get their hands on one.

Nikon Rumors reports that Nikon’s Sales Support team in the United Kingdom communicated that the Nikon D850 is “now end of life,” which effectively means it is discontinued.

“We would like to inform you that the D850 model is now end of life. Unfortunately, we are not expecting any further stock, and as a result, we are not accepting new orders. Please update your systems accordingly. We apologize for any inconvenience. If you have any questions, please let us know,” Nikon’s UK Sales Team said in an email.

This aligns with the UK retail situation, where stock varies by retailer. For example, Wex, a major UK photo retailer, no longer lists the D850. However, as Digicame-Info reports, the D850 is still available in Japan, and it remains easy to find in the United States as well.

There are a couple of caveats here. First, as PetaPixel has seen plenty of times, cameras and lenses are often discontinued in one region before another. Second, nothing may have actually changed regarding Nikon’s manufacturing of the D850. The company could have halted production a while ago, and local stock has only just run dry in the UK, prompting the new notice.

PetaPixel has reached out to Nikon for clarification and will update this story when more information becomes available.

In the meantime, photographers can still acquire the Nikon D850. Even if new stock runs out, this prolific DSLR is widely available on the used market.

As for brand-new units, they remain readily available in the United States. B&H still carries the Nikon D850, for instance, and has it discounted by $300 through November 29 for the holidays. Nikon USA also still sells the D850 directly.

The Nikon D850 remains a fantastic camera that photographers still love, and it will stay easy to buy for the foreseeable future. The only real question is how much longer it will be available brand-new in the box—a status that will eventually end everywhere, not just in the UK.

#9049. Desai Chia designs Bethesda Residence to balance "openness and discretion"

A large light well brings daylight deep into this private home that was designed by Desai Chia Architecture for a tight site in a dense Maryland neighbourhood.

The project takes its name from its location in Bethesda, a city located northwest of Washington DC.

“Its compact lot and the close proximity of neighbouring houses required a careful response balancing both openness and discretion.”

The architects intended the house to “rethink suburban-urban hybrid living through a modern lens”.

Roughly rectangular in plan, it has three levels and a basement. Setbacks help break up the mass, particularly on the street-facing elevation.

The building appears “as a two-storey building from several vantage points,” the team said.

“The home is carefully scaled to blend with neighbouring houses, balancing a strong architectural identity with sensitivity to its suburban context,” the team said.

Facades are clad in grey fibre-cement panels made to last for a century. The material is known for protecting against fire, pests and extreme weather, according to the team.

“A durable, low-maintenance exterior with a strong architectural presence was a key client priority from the outset,” the architects said.

“Glass-fibre-reinforced concrete (GRFC) panels were selected to create a crisp, sculptural facade that captures texture and shifting light throughout the day.”

A modern-style bay window adds dimension and visual interest to the front and back facades.

Within the home, public spaces are located on the ground level. The rear portion opens into a yard with a lap pool.

The upper levels contain bedrooms and two offices, and the top floor has a rooftop terrace. The basement holds a gym, ping-pong area and media room.

“This vertical, faceted volume allows sunlight to cascade downward, distributing diffuse light from a small skylight across circulation spaces on multiple levels while minimising solar heat gain,” Desai Chia Architecture said.

The all-electric house has a geothermal heating and cooling system. To enable the homeowners to age in place, the house has a shaft where an ADA-compliant elevator could be added in the future.

The homeowners are physicians, one of whom can walk to his practice in downtown Bethesda.

“When needed, the dedicated home offices allow both physicians to work from home in spaces with calming natural light,” the studio said.

“Its location – easily walkable to downtown amenities and robust public transit – supports a connected pattern of work and family life.”

Other homes in Maryland include a restored carriage house by Colleen Healey Architecture that features colourful facade panels and a family home by Ziger Snead clad in stone shingles, charred wood and weathering steel.

Design architect: Desai Chia ArchitectureArchitect of record: Thomson & Cooke Architects

#9047. PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH is best known for camera bags, tripods and straps, and in the phone world for telephoto extender lenses designed for Vivo and Oppo flagships. Its RetroVa kit brings that lens work to the iPhone.

The system first appeared on Kickstarter in January 2026 for the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro families, combining a camera-style Bluetooth grip, retro-style case, and a 2.35x teleconverter for the phone’s telephoto lens. The newest version designed for the iPhone 17 Pro/Pro Max and 18 Pro/Pro Max series brings in a lighter and smaller 2X lens, along with a 4X telephoto lens as an alternative.

This all provides focal range that simply doesn’t work as well when using the phone itself. With 200mm, 235mm, and 400mm equivalents, the iPhone can reach farther with more optical clarity. A dedicated app also offers old school film simulations and manual controls for composition to let you decide how you want your images to look.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set comes in Graphite Black, while the 4X lens, grip, and the case are also sold separately and in smaller bundles, offering users different ways to put the kit together.

RetroVa Black Friday deal: From November 19 to 30, the RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set (Graphite Black, iPhone 17/18 Pro Max) is 10% off, and PetaPixel readers can take an extra 10% off with code BYTEDDYK. Buy it on Amazon or directly from PGYTECH.

The Ultimate Gift Set brings them all together in the box: the 4X telephoto lens, a lens adapter bracket, lens pouch, RetroVa phone case, grip, a photography strap, and an Arca-Swiss compatible tripod collar for the lens. The case is polycarbonate and works with MagSafe, leaving the proverbial door open for additional magnetic accessories. Though it has a lip over the edges, you can still use the case with a screen protector on the phone itself.

The lightweight grip weighs 63 grams for the Pro and 65.4 grams for the Pro Max. It carries physical controls, a built-in microSD slot, and a standard 1/4-inch socket on the base for tripods and monopods. It slides into the phone’s USB-C port with a lock switch that holds it firmly in place, though it actually pairs and connects to the device via Bluetooth.

It’s important to get the right size because there are separate variants for the Pro and Pro Max. While the lens mount is the same on either build, you can’t slide a Pro grip into the Pro Max, for instance. That also goes for the case, which is the most integral piece because that’s what everything else in the kit attaches to. Fortunately, since the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro models share the same dimensions, you don’t need to worry about compatibility in that regard.

The shutter button functions a lot like a typical camera would: half-press to focus, press to take the shot, or hold it down for a burst. The zoom lever right under it can either skip between focal lengths in Vintage mode or adjust zoom more freely in the Standard setting. Below that is the control dial that you can choose to adjust exposure, ISO, white balance, or shutter speed. Lastly, the multi-function button acts as power on/off, switches modes, and sets up Bluetooth pairing. A small LED next to it indicates pairing and a solid connection.

The microSD card slot (UHS-I or UHS-II) underneath is another handy way to save excess photos or video, albeit with some key parameters. You can readily save RAW photos or 4K video to it, only you’re limited to HEVC-coded footage and max 120fps. Plug the grip into a laptop where you can then offload the content directly.

If you record in Apple’s Camera app, video automatically goes to the card when you use supported formats, while PGYTECH’s app supports more recording formats. Even third-party apps that can record to external storage can recognize the card, too.

PGYTECH also makes 62mm and 67mm filter adapter rings sold separately from the available kits. They’re not included in any of them, though will work just fine with any filters in those two respective sizes. Being a separate piece, you just slide out the lens adapter ring and bring in the filter adapter instead. There is no way to use a filter with the teleconverter lenses themselves, since the filter adapter covers the iPhone’s entire rear array.

PGYTECH designed the kit to work with a dedicated companion app called PGYTECH: Pro Camera & Editor. It’s free to download, only requiring iOS 17 or later to run. You do, however, need to be diligent about keeping it up to date because if you don’t, the app may lock you out of all the manual control settings. A pop-up notice stating that a subscription is required to unlock those pro features isn’t actually necessary. Update the app and that message disappears.

While there is an Auto mode available, Manual provides controls for exposure, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, tint, and filters, which you can then map to the grip by going to Settings->Hardware Settings. You will need to ensure the grip is on and once connected via Bluetooth, select RetroVa in the drop-down menu to pick what you want. At any point within that section, you can always look at tutorials on connecting the grip and a video FAQ as well.

Unless you explicitly make your own manual adjustments, the app’s camera interface treats everything as if it was in Auto. So, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, and tint will all dynamically shift based on what’s in frame. Tap to focus works just like any other camera app would. One difference, though, is if you have Focus Assist on (focus peaking by another name), you will see where the camera is actually focusing after you tap, giving you an indication of where the focal plane is.

Other manual controls, like a histogram and priority facial recognition (the camera will always focus on a face first in this setting), are elective. Standard bits, like a timer, live photo, watermark, and aspect ratio (1:1, 4:3, and 16:9) round out much of what’s left. There is a Dive Mode that switches controls to physical buttons for underwater photos and video, while also applying an “underwater filter” as a copy of the original when captured. You can make separate manual settings adjustments for this mode, too.

In addition to about 15 standard filters, PGYTECH offers a series of nostalgic film simulations, ranging from Classic Negative and Nostalgic Negative to Kodak Gold 200, Fujifilm PRO Neg Std, Velvia 100, Classic Chrome, FujiColor C200, Tungsten 500, and Bleach Bypass. Choose any one at any time and adjust the intensity from 0-100. These simulations apply no matter what image format you shoot with and aren’t limited to still photos: they work with video, too.

The app includes a Retro Film mode that features the same set of film simulations, except it changes the hybrid zoom ranges to include 35mm and 50mm equivalents to better match traditional prime lenses. Otherwise, images process the same way as the Photo mode.

It’s also possible to apply any of these filters on a photo after you capture it within the in-app editing suite, including HSL for some color grading. Beauty features also present a variety of options for those seeking that kind of detail. Under Creative, there are templates for sharing or social media.

An on-device AI tool in the Adjust section lets you try enhancing detail in images by either using HD to improve clarity or AI HD to restore detail in softer images. You need to download it to make it work on-device rather than in the cloud but once it’s there, you can utilize it any time. If you’d rather avoid AI completely, you don’t have to use it.

Mind you, you’re not forced into PGYTECH’s app for basic shooting (without the lenses) since the grip also works with the native Camera app. To make that work with iOS, go to the Settings app, then Accessibility->Zoom->toggle On->Full Screen Zoom. At that point, having already paired it to the phone, you gain access to Apple’s own Camera app where pressing the shutter or zooming in responds onscreen. PGYTECH says it’s working on more third-party app integrations, so we’ll see where that leads.

The 4X lens is both the newest and the headline of the trio. It uses an 11-element, 3-group optical design with fluorite-grade low-dispersion glass and weighs about 137 grams. It feels sturdy in hand, which is why it’s smart to use it with the tripod collar when you need to prop it up for a long exposure or timelapse.

It’s a 400mm equivalent optical focal length, going up to 1200mm with a digital crop. The 4x lens also comes with a case and slightly different bracket that also includes a mount for the iPhone’s main camera. That gives you a 240mm optical equivalent or 400mm with an in-sensor crop with more background separation, which PGYTECH pitches for portraits.

The 2x lens, at about 104 grams, gives 200mm optical and 400mm cropped over the telephoto camera, or 105mm and 200mm over the main camera. This lens doesn’t come with a case but does include the same lens bracket the Ultimate Gift Set does, which only covers the phone’s telephoto camera. That’s an important distinction if you’re looking to use any of the lenses on both the main and telephoto cameras.

In the case of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the PGYTECH app can’t control the main camera’s mechanical aperture, so you can’t benefit from stopping down to f/4 for certain photo or video opportunities. Either way, all three lenses fit any of the RetroVa cases and brackets made for the iPhone.

One thing to always keep in mind is how much attaching the lenses considerably increases minimum focusing distance. PGYTECH lists 16.2 meters for the 4x over the telephoto camera and three meters over the main camera, against 5.22 meters and 60 centimeters for the 2x. There’s no optical image stabilization in any of them, so PGYTECH relies on its app’s stabilization algorithm for steadier handheld results. Handheld, the kit is better now than it was just a few months ago.

There’s nothing electronic communicating between the lenses and the app, so you have to manually select the lens you’re using and then turn that off or switch if you end up putting on another one. Doing so makes corresponding changes to available focal lengths and ensures focusing and processing fall in line with what you’re using. It’s one of the easiest things to forget while shooting with it in the field but it’s vitally important.

Technically, the lenses aren’t supposed to work with Apple’s own app, though I randomly found no obstruction in doing so. Other times, it didn’t work at all. This has nothing to do with the kit and everything to do with how Apple engineers its camera array. Because it functions as one virtual system, the software can decide what it thinks is the best camera, even though you’ve already chosen one over another. PGYTECH’s app doesn’t do that, leaning purely on whichever camera you’ve attached the lens to capture images or video.

If you get lucky enough to make Apple’s app work, it gives you access to manual controls (in the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max) as well as the possibility of manipulating the variable aperture with the main camera. It’s just a very hit-or-miss proposition, so your experience may truly vary.

As a kit, the RetroVa is trying to present a camera-like feel to capturing photos and video on the iPhone. That’s the basic gist, but in practice, the handling offers a fairly high degree of versatility in both perspective and ergonomics. Without having to stretch out a thumb or finger to hit the onscreen shutter, the grip’s controls make low or high-angle shots easier to manage. Double-clicking the iPhone’s Camera Control will launch Apple’s Camera app but if you prefer to switch that to PGYTECH’s app within iOS, go to Settings->Camera->Camera Control and tap on it to make that the default.

In the four months I’ve been using the kit (both with the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro), multiple updates over that time have either added new features or refined existing ones. One thing you have to always remember is that this app processes images slower than Apple’s app does, especially when shooting in ProRAW. You can see that in the preview window where a yellow indicator shows that it’s rendering what you just shot.

The reason that matters is because it’s easy to ruin a photo by quickly moving the camera after capture. That very brief window between snapping the shutter and seeing the resulting image populate the preview window can feel like an eternity when shooting action, like I did at multiple WNBA games with this kit. It’s faster if you’re purely shooting JPEG or HEIF but the same thing can happen if you’re a little too eager to see what you just got.

Part of what PGYTECH is up against is the smaller 1/2.55-inch sensor Apple uses for the telephoto camera on both the 17 Pro and 18 Pro series. Adding significant optics to that lens certainly gets you closer to the subject or action but it’s best to also learn the subtleties of PGYTECH’s app. Lighting conditions are of paramount importance, as noise can creep in at higher ISO levels when you need to raise the shutter speed.

While you can shoot in either ProRAW, JPEG, or HEIF at either 12 or 48-megapixels, you don’t really wield any outsized control over the imaging pipeline. Apple’s processing engine still kicks in, forcing you to lean more on RAW images if you feel more comfortable with the higher degree of manual control available. PGYTECH isn’t necessarily only targeting seasoned mobile photographers with the RetroVa kit but it’s still worth dealing with the learning curve.

The controls include manual focus, with focus peaking as an elective option where you get to choose between red, green, or blue as the visual aid. It applies no matter if you’re tapping to focus manually or adjusting it in the slider. One key tidbit is tapping to focus doesn’t always work as you’d expect because focal length (even for the iPhone’s own lenses) behave natively. Within the app, there’s no fusion between them to enable, say, macro shooting at closer distances where the main or ultra-wide might step in to help the cause.

All that aside, the handling is a big part of the appeal here. As a slab device, the iPhone can prove tough to work with under different perspective and angles, so the grip turns it into something you can maneuver in more interesting ways. With a finger on the shutter and the ability to make granular adjustments with the dial, plus the strap to take off the weight, the creative possibilities certainly stand out.

Focusing is the biggest challenge because subject tracking isn’t the same as Apple’s own implementation, and you often still need to tap on the screen to hone in on what you want the composition to look like. One workaround for that is to get a separate screen primarily used for rear camera selfies as a way to wirelessly compose a shot when it’s hard to contort yourself to see the real time preview on the phone.

PGYTECH says it’s working on tracking autofocus and on controlling the iPhone’s aperture from the grip, which would address two key challenges in using the RetroVa kit. A universal lens adapter and further lens types are also on PGYTECH’s wish list, though no firm commitment.

For now, RetroVa is an iPhone-only system built around the Pro and Pro Max models, albeit with some nuances noted earlier. Not everything made for the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro series applies to what’s available for the iPhone 16 Pro series.

It’s also worth noting the kit isn’t a qualitative replacement for a mirrorless camera. The iPhone’s image sensors aren’t in the same league to begin with, but the app’s manual controls are far more extensive and the lenses a big upgrade over the awful hybrid crops the iPhone offers on its own. Compared to a bigger mirrorless, however, this kit is easier to carry, especially when you take off the lenses.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set is 10% off through November 30, plus an extra 10% with code BYTEDDYK, on Amazon and at PGYTECH.

#9046. After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens

Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project. It is the first time the museum, founded in 1874 and nestled into the rock of the storied Acropolis hill, has been accessible to the public since 2007.

The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.

Once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill. This offered larger and state-of-the-art space in which to house the antiquities from the Parthenon and other Greek sites, as well as a viewing room designed for the Elgin Marbles—currently showing casts, but with the idea that one day the museum might one day welcome the real items.

The Old Acropolis Museum was left empty for years, and plans eventually developed to use it as storage and administrative spaces. But by 2019, the Greek state definitively nixed this idea.

“For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its unique location, should be converted into offices and storage facilities,” said Mendoni during her opening speech. “We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose. However, it was not to become just another conventional museum, but rather a museum and exhibition space hosting exhibitions on the history, archaeology and culture of Athens, as well as contemporary art exhibitions inspired by Greek civilisation and innovative programmes incorporating cutting-edge technology.”

The museum will now host both a rotating selection of artefacts as well as a contemporary art programme. The first exhibition, Athens City Idea, focuses on Athens as a social, political, and economic entity, via tragic masks, statues, coins, and amphorae that have been in storage elsewhere across Athens, plus recent discoveries. A digital art component animated the Parthenon’s friezes and the history of the Acropolis Hill.

Part of the idea behind the temporary exhibitions is to keep the museum’s display current, a point also underlined by its commitment to contemporary art.

This includes the last of a trilogy of works commissioned for Athens from the American artist Michael Rakowitz, which is also the final project of Neon, the roving art foundation created by Dimitris Daskalopoulos that for 14 years has funded art and exhibitions across the city, and which announced its closure earlier this year.

“You could say that the first contemporary work here was Phidias’s statue of Athena in the 5th century BCE,” quipped Daskalopoulos, the Athens-born collector who founded Neon. Daskalopoulos also supported the refurbishment of the Old Acropolis Museum, which was funded by both private and public money. “But encouraging the coexistence of antiquity with the contemporary is a challenge we have embraced many times throughout our work at Neon.”

Michael Rakowitz and Elina Kountouri, the director of Neon, outside the reopened Old Acropolis Museum

Rakowitz’s installation What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026), which was commissioned by Neon, and comprises a kiln and newly fired bricks, looks at a lesser-known episode in the Acropolis’s history.

“I realised that you could only tell the whole story of the site if you look through the lens of migration,” the artist told The Art Newspaper. He studied the population exchanges during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, when Greece and Turkey forced a combined total of around 1.5 million inhabitants to leave—Christian Turks to Greece and Muslim Greeks to Turkey. When the Turkish refugees arrived in Athens, they set up tents and encampments at the base of the Acropolis hill.

“Thinking about a ruin as being something that can renew itself to a population and become once again a shelter excited me,” he said. "When I found out about the tradition of the Asia Minor refugees who were able to go back to Turkey after some years, and then the Muslims who were uprooted from Greece, when those populations were able to visit their the departed homelands, they found oftentimes their buildings or towns in a state of ruin, and they would take a brick from that place and bring it back as a memento.”

Installation view of Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

Rakowitz has incorporated these original bricks alongside ones newly made with inscriptions and stamps that bear witness to more recent histories of displacement. For these he worked with survivors of the 1920s population transfers as well as women in the Melissa Network, a nonprofit organisation that supports migrant women in Greece.

“I wanted these bricks to become a foundation for a new kind of city that welcomes strangers and doesn't push them back at sea,” he said.

After sponsoring many exhibitions and commissions across his native Greece, Neon founder Dimitris Daskalopoulos will continue to fund individual projects in Athens and several curatorial posts

Pandermalis, a revered archaeologist and professor, had also been outspoken in calling for the reunification of all the Parthenon marbles in Athens

Athens are still hopeful that the marbles will be returned, to be be housed in the currently unfinished New Acropolis Museum

The Acropolis museum is under construction, and the design for the permanent exhibition is in preparation

#9044. Adobe's Creative Agent transforms Creative Cloud tools and Firefly workflows

Adobe has rolled out its Creative Agent across the Creative Cloud, providing users with agentic workflows across its platforms to give creatives “more time for their craft”.

Unveiled at the Adobe MAX conference in Miami Beach on 10 November, the update spans the brand’s flagship Creative Cloud tools.

Photoshop now features generative restyle and relight, Premiere has a new colour mode, and InDesign now supports co-editing (beta).

Adobe is also bringing the Creative Agent to Firefly – its AI creative studio – through the Firefly AI Assistant, which is currently in beta.

Users can direct the assistant in plain language, with Adobe stating it has already been used for everything from batch retouching portraits to turning product shots into short-form social videos.

The aim is to help creators take on projects that may previously have required more time, resources or technical complexity.

Adobe has also launched Firefly Design in beta, a single workspace that combines raster and vector graphics with motion, 3D and print design.

Available as part of Creative Cloud, Firefly Design allows designers to build, review, and hand over projects without leaving the platform.

Topaz Labs, now part of Adobe, has released two new image-enhancement models, Wonder 4 and Image HDR, which are sold separately through Topaz.

Adobe said the Creative Cloud updates respond to the way creatives are increasingly working – juggling more formats, apps and mediums while being asked to turn projects around faster.

The brand’s latest approach aims to tackle this by bringing “AI assistance and collaboration directly into the Adobe tools they rely on”.

Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for Creative Cloud at Adobe, said the aim is to protect what makes a creative’s work distinctive.

“The ideas, taste, style and vision that creative professionals bring to their work are what make their work stand out,” said Subramaniam.

“Our latest Creative Cloud innovations transform our trusted creative tools into agentic, intelligent workflows that give pros the precision, control and flexibility to explore their ideas, streamline their work and stay focused on the creative decisions that make their work uniquely theirs.”

The Creative Agent – which Adobe describes as a creative partner – now powers AI Assistants (currently in beta) across Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io. In Photoshop, the assistant is available only in the Photoshop beta app.

The agent handles multi-step tasks behind the scenes, letting professionals delegate work and increase their creative velocity while remaining “in the director’s chair”.

In Premiere, the agent now supports new capabilities, including applying an effect to every clip in a sequence, tracking a masked subject through a frame, and adjusting colour and exposure across a whole sequence at once.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations, which allow external AI agents to connect with its software.

The integrations will let users instruct third-party agents of their choice to work inside Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, editing project files directly on their own computer.

Layers, vectors and sequences stay fully editable throughout the process, so users can “step in at any moment to refine the work by hand”. The local MCP integrations will be available in private beta in early 2027.

If a user’s chosen third-party agent is also connected to other MCP-capable tools, such as Google Drive or Slack, it can bring them into the same workflow. For example, it could pull in a brief from Google Docs, work on the project using Adobe’s tools and share the result with colleagues in Slack.

Adobe has also added several updates that give Firefly users more say over how the AI assistant works. Creatives are now able to save their preferred formats, colours, brand guidelines, characters and products to be applied consistently in future projects.

A new plan mode lets users review, edit and approve the agent’s plan before it starts, or leave the agent to run on its own. Adobe explained that creators remain in control, “guiding the work and making creative decisions as their projects evolve”.

Users can also choose which AI model the agent works with, or let the agent select the best fit for the task.

In Firefly Boards, the agent can help develop mood boards, storyboards and concepts through conversation as they take shape in real time, “guided by human taste and direction”.

Adobe also introduced a preview of always-on agents to carry out routine jobs, such as sorting new files or preparing content for different platforms, “even when the customer steps away”.

Firefly’s video, design and image editors have also been updated, with the aim of taking projects from initial idea to finished work in a single workflow.

Among the other additions are a gallery of ready-made, quick actions, visual boards, and node-bases workflows through Firefly Graph (beta), which lets users build repeatable workflows of their own.

Adobe’s examples include turning a video storyboard into a finished cut and, in Firefly Design, carrying a brand identity from initial concept through client review within a single design workspace.

#9042. Ahead of Taiwan local elections, politicians crowd in at Art Taipei

This year's edition of Taiwan's 34-year-old fair Art Taipei (29 October to 2 November) and its third concurrent Taipei Art Week (TAW) fell, serendipitously, just before the alleged spying scandal that emerged around Taiwan's celebrated native son, the naturalised American Nvidia mogul Jensen Huang. This spared fair sales the ensuing worldwide tech stock dive. Rather, concerns during the fair focused more on the pending midterm elections on 28 November.

The fair's opening ceremony was thick with politicians. Prominent figures included incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, now in a close re-election race, who would days later face protests at the Taipei Pride parade and festival over his police department's aggressive raid of gay bar Commander D on 3 October. Taiwan's minister of culture Li Yuan heralded his department's successful efforts in September to get a pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale named for Taiwan rather than the sponsoring institution, which sparked a diplomatic row with mainland China, and pronounced that "AI will not replace artists!"

"The presence of political figures at art fairs is a familiar feature of Taiwan's cultural landscape," says Claudia Chen, director of Art Taipei, chair of its organiser, the Taipei Art Gallery Association (Taga), and cofounder of Taipei's Liang Gallery. She adds that it builds public visibility and engagement for the cultural sector. "We hope this attention can help deepen public understanding of the art market and highlight its close connections with cultural development, urban growth, and international exchange."

The question, she continues, "is whether this engagement with political leaders can translate into consistent policy support, particularly in areas such as arts education, international promotion, and incentives for private collecting and cultural patronage." Taiwan lags behind most East Asian governments in cultural investment. "We hope cultural development can become an important public issue and receive sustained support across political parties, allowing Taiwan to gradually translate its economic strength into a deeper and more far-reaching cultural influence."

Chen says that Taiwan's technology sector and the private wealth it fuels "provide an important foundation for its art market. However, translating economic growth into greater activity in the art market takes time," as well as innovation and outreach by galleries.

The 127 galleries that Art Taipei welcomed to the Taipei World Trade Center this year included the return of influential galleries such as Richard Koh Fine Art, from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, for the first time post-pandemic, and Perrotin for a third consecutive year. Newcomers included Tokyo's Misako & Rosen. One of Taipei's leading platforms, Tina Keng Gallery (TKG+) and TKG+ Projects, joined for the first time in about five years. "In recent years, with Singapore, Seoul, Hong Kong, there is a lot happening, so we needed an opportunity to do a Taiwan show," says the gallery's assistant to the director, Alice Liang. With the suspension of the sleeker international fair Taipei Dangdai after 2025, Art Taipei has resumed its status as the main "hometown" option, she says.

Sales of a "museum-type" installation of works by artists including Sanyu, Kuo Tzumin and Michael Lin went "pretty well", says Liang. "People were surprised and curious," with "positive feedback" from collectors who skewed young and were both Taiwanese and foreign. She adds that the launch of the broader art week had little impact on sales, "but we can feel the difference, with the events, parties and open studios."

Fair organisers also report a generational shift among buyers, with 20.8% of those surveyed saying they were attending for the first or second time, double the figure for 2023. VIP collectors also declined from 77.5% to 54.2%, suggesting that the publicly accessible side of the art week is also providing outreach for the fair. Endeavours included five bus rounds, guided tours, digital art screenings at Taipei Lumitree and 30 public artworks displayed citywide, says Chen. For the art industry, a forum included speakers such as M+ Hong Kong curator Russell Storer and 2026 Venice Biennale Korea Pavilion curator Binna Choi.

The fair also featured an expanded presence of galleries from Korea and Japan, with 25 and 22 respectively, drawing on Taga's ongoing collaboration with those countries' gallery associations. Galleries from Japan, Taiwan's former coloniser, "have maintained a longstanding presence in the Taiwanese market, with many having established strong collector networks and brand recognition over the years," says Chen. The Korean presence "demonstrates the Korean art industry's capacity to expand into international markets through collaboration."

Tastes at the fair are also shifting towards Pop and contemporary art, says dealer Steven Chen (no relation). His Taipei gallery Yiyun Art has attended the fair for seven of the past ten years. It represents traditional Asian paintings, which remain a major sector at Art Taipei, if reduced from previous years. His dramatic maze of a booth, evoking a Chinese scholar's garden, saw steady crowds and sales, including of a painting by Yu Cheng Yao for $90,000. "With the young generation is coming more to the fair," says Chen, "we need a new language on ink art. It is the same culture with a new expression."

Claudia Chen says that Taiwan's collectors are maintaining "purchasing momentum" but have become increasingly deliberate, needing time and established relationships with galleries. Meanwhile, younger collectors are "gradually entering the market, bringing more diverse perspectives shaped by their own lifestyles and aesthetic preferences."

#9041. Jabez Bartlett channels “brutalist-folk” spirit for debut furniture collection

Photography by George Darrell unless stated otherwise

The London maker of Milan design week’s much-discussed inflatable coffee table has unveiled his debut furniture collection, which includes veiny wax chairs and a rug adorned with cattle tags.

Jabez Bartlett is a British production-turned-furniture designer who caused a stir during April’s Milan design week, where he showed a pillowy PVC coffee table topped with an opalescent resin surface.

A circular version followed, and both pieces are part of The Freight Proportioned to the Groove, an exhibition of his debut furniture collection that opens today in Hackney, London.

Bartlett told Dezeen that he wanted to start creating furniture to experiment with materials that he has used to bring film sets to life on screen.

“With set design, things don’t necessarily have to be practical,” said the Devon-born designer. “It’s all about how they look on camera. I wanted to play with this in a more material and physical world.”

“There’s a lot of industrial materials we’ve always used that I think are incredibly beautiful,” he continued. “It’s interesting to use something heavy and practical in a luxury piece.”

Bartlett’s collection includes a triptych of marbled dining chairs made from a mixture of microcrystalline and crude oil wax cast in plywood frames.

The pieces were informed by a Japanese games table owned by the designer, characterised by a gridded top.

“I had the idea to remake it as a giant candle, with a wick in each square,” he explained. The idea became three chunky chairs that resemble large candles, embellished with playful wicks.

Bartlett’s collection also features a trio of lighting pieces clad in stretchy latex skins.

The smallest is a ceramic table lamp with a bloated shade, while the other two are angular floor lamps supported by metal structures, one of which was on display at the southwest London gallery Saatchi Yates earlier this year.

Despite their industrial materials, Bartlett also considers his pieces as nods to the wilderness.

“I started off wanting to make brutalist-folk furniture, and now I’m seeing it, I feel like I got there,” he said. “Memory and illusion play a big part, and of course, growing up in Devon leaves an imprint of the natural and the ancient world on you.”

Another of the collection’s pieces is a large diamond-patterned textile rug, overdyed and bleached, and embellished with metal tags normally used to identify cattle.

The tags hem the rug and were also embroidered into its fabric in decorative circles.

Also on display in the exhibition are a monolithic cast acrylic mirror, a glossy black plinth and column with protruding thorns and another floor lamp with a similarly spiky, elongated black body and a sandy leather shade.

The title of Bartlett’s exhibition refers to the final line of poet Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century poem, That Love is All There Is.

The Freight Proportioned to the Groove is on display from 26 to 29 November at Tuscany Wharf, 4B Orsman Road, London N1 5QJ. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
