#9024. Meet BC Architects & Studies & Materials, Marina Tabassum's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler, two of BC Architects & Studies & Materials’ founders discuss how their ideas have gone from being perceived as the product of “young idealism” to being taken seriously by the construction sector.

The Brussels-based studio is at the forefront of bio-regional and circular design, with a whole arm of its practice dedicated to the development of new materials, often making use of construction waste.

Recently, the studio worked with UK studio Assemble and circular design lab Atelier Luma to create Le Magasin Électrique at Luma Arles in France, with a palette that included everything from rammed earth and construction waste to salt and algae.

Alongside these likeminded practitioners, BC Architects & Studies & Materials is at the forefront of a recent wave of interest in bio-based materials and vernacular methods – ideas that the studio has been championing for some 15 years, pushing for systemic change in the industry.

Founded between 2009 and 2012 by Ken De Cooman, Wes Degreef, Nicolas Coeckelberghs and Laurens Bekemans, the origins of BC Architects & Studies & Materials were – as its tripartite name suggests – not particularly conventional.

The studio is comprised of three different legal entities: BC Architects, an architecture cooperative; BC Studies, a non-profit “education laboratory”; and BC Materials, a material production co-operative.

BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s approach and outlook was borne out of a series of early projects in Burundi, Morocco and Ethiopia – where the studio briefly had a satellite office – which were grounded in working with local communities and materials.

“A lot of our first experiences in architecture were linked to different construction cultures,” said De Cooman. “I lived in Ethiopia for five years, others were in Morocco for a long time, and at the same time, we were finding our way in Belgium.”

“It was a different path to learning architecture as a practitioner,” he continued. We learnt to work with local materials and short supply chains, to make do with what you find around.”

The studio’s first built project was the Library of Muyinga in Burundi, developed using an open-source template from the OpenStructures network and constructed from compressed earth bricks alongside members of the local community.

It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture

BC Architects & Studies & Materials also designed several school buildings and a women’s shelter in Morocco, often using the construction process itself as an opportunity for the sharing of knowledge around vernacular construction techniques and materials.

According to De Cooman, however, this strand of the studio’s work was never intended to be long-term.

Challenging a tendency in the industry to view these methods and techniques as solely belonging to the realm of “humanitarian” architecture, BC Architects & Studies & Materials’s aim was to apply them to the business-as-usual processes of architecture and construction back home in Belgium.

“It feels much more valid to be doing this in our own construction culture,” said De Cooman.

“It was a huge learning process, and now we’re really focussing on the here and now because it’s here that we need to actually change the most.”

While a big part of this change is the studio’s use of alternative materials, it was also based on the idea of building being an opportunity for shared learning, driven by BC’s belief in the the need for architects to be more engaged with the construction process.

We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other field

Several of the studio’s early projects in Belgium the result of these learning workshops. Maison de Chasse, a rammed-earth hunting house, was constructed over the course of the first rammed earth workshop in Belgium, based on the techniques of Martin Rauch and Anna Heringer.

In 2017, the renovation of a series of warehouses in Ghent into an artist’s studio for Pascale Marthine Tayou was achieved via a five-week “Urban Construction Camp”, in which volunteers created a new hempcrete structure inside an existing metal shell.

“We’re still trying to emulate what our first experiences were: creating shared learning environments with people that can bring together different skills and learn from each other by really engaging with other fields, not on paper, but with the heart and the hands included,” explained De Cooman.

“It is crazy that we now have a system where, as an architect, you draw all the execution files and send them to a contractor to execute it exactly how you drew it.”

“The magic happens when everyone can get together – you can draw it together, find a passionate contractor to make it with.”

BC Architects & Studies & Materials was keen, however, to not be defined by this smaller-scale work, with the whole point being to demonstrate how these techniques and materials could be scaled up into larger contexts.

The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings

A key means to achieving this was the formal establishing of BC Materials in 2018, enabled by the interest generated by their earlier projects. Alongside consultancy, workshops and training, the BC Materials arm also offers its own range of earth and clay products, Léém.

“The idea of BC is to not only do small projects but also to change the building culture by making these materials available to big contractors and buildings,” says Wes Degreef.

“I think we were very surprised that the idea of working with a certain bioregion and its materials is something that we forgot in Europe.”

“Some of it still exists, but you really have to search for it. And with earth materials, for example, those crafts don’t exist anymore in Belgium. So we had to do it; we became the craftsmen.”

Sure enough, the scale of the projects involving BC Architects & Studies & Materials – whether they are engaged as architects or as craftspeople – is growing.

“In the beginning, we were just like young, crazy people who are doing these weird things on Belgium,” said De Cooman.

“There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium.”

There was a bit of interest in it, but it was also seen as, young, idealist energy. Now, we’re operating at a scale where we are actually seen as serious partners in the construction sector here in Belgium

In Brussels, BC Architects & Studies & Materials worked alongside EVR-architecten to convert a former barracks into the Usquare Feder university district, the materials for which were sourced in part by the dismantling of several neighbouring buildings.

With numerous other residential and office projects in the works – including a new bioregional materials hub and workspace in the centre of Brussels, Stadsatelierdeville, that will be its future office.

If it at times felt like BC Architects & Studies & Materials were up against the world, it is projects like La Magasin Électrique, which was a finalist for the 2026 Mies van Der Rohe Award, that reveal a growing international network who share their outlook, one that De Cooman is quick to credit with a lot of their own success.

“I think the dial is shifting, but I don’t think it is us who did it,” said De Cooman.

“There are all kinds of practises, organisations, material developers, and so on, who see a different construction sector – it’s a wave, a societal shift.”

“We’re very happy about it, but it’s broader than our practice. The construction sector is very conservative and we’re not there yet at all.”

Degreef adds that external social and economic pressures have also had a hand in forcing change to some degree.

“After Covid and the impacts on material prices, the gap between contemporary materials and the materials we want to promote is not so big anymore.”

Asked if there is a particular type of building that represents a dream project, however, they remain resolutely focused on processes and systems.

“I think, for us, it’s not in the buildings itself. It’s not what we build, but how we build and how everybody needs to build.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#9023. charred wooden modules conceal six-sided mirror chamber inside interactive play installation

alchemy is a two-module free-play installation that guides children and adults through dark inflatable chambers, a six-sided mirror room, and a pink recycled foam space.

Florian López edited by christina vergopoulou November 26, 2026 3 min

Designed by Florian López, Alchemy is an interactive free-play installation for children and adults that organizes an exhibition space as an anatomical body to be traversed. The structure comprises two architectural modules linked by tubular conduits and clad on the exterior in timber treated with the Japanese yakisugi charring technique, creating a blackened, fissured surface that functions as a protective outer skin. Circular openings cut into the charred facades act as physical thresholds into a three-stage interior sequence.

The first module begins in darkness, housing black inflatable volumes shaped after intestinal forms and kept in continuous motion by a steady airflow to create a soft, enveloping environment. From there, visitors pass into a six-sided mirrored chamber that multiplies reflections across all surfaces, shifting perspective and spatial awareness.

Crossing into the second module, the designer shifts the interior from individual perception to collaborative assembly. Lined with pink recycled rebonded foam referencing internal flesh and muscle tissue, the room is stocked with loose geometric blocks without prescriptive instructions, inviting children and adults to negotiate and build shared structures through open-ended play.

a six-sided mirrored room multiplies visitors’ reflections from every anglethe mirror chamber alters spatial perception along the routeblack inflatable volumes anchor Alchemy’s dark chambercircular apertures cut into the frame to connect each chamber to the nextthe interactive installation is organized as an anatomical sequence

#9021. Rachel Whiteread Has Designed the 2027 Brit Awards Trophy

Dame Rachel Whiteread, who was the first woman artist to win the Turner Prize in 1993, has been selected to design the 2027 Brit Awards trophy. The trophy has previously been designed by the likes of Damien Hirst, Zaha Hadid, Es Devlin and Anish Kapoor.

The trophy will be bestowed upon musicians nominated for the prestigious award ceremony taking place on February 27, 2027. Each trophy takes inspiration from the image of Britannia, a tall, elegant female figure that personifies Britain. For her design, Whiteread has inverted the statue, exposing its silver lining with punched holes throughout. “I exposed the interior of the statue—as an artist would do with their music,” said the artist in a statement. “I accepted the invitation to design next year’s Brit Award trophy, as I saw this as a natural extension of my work—to continue to celebrate and recognize British art and creativity, and to have an opportunity to apply my own perspective within such an iconic British cultural institution.” Related Articles Nnena Kalu Wins Turner Prize, Becoming First Learning-Disabled Artist to Take UK's Top Art Award Rachel Whiteread's Collaboration with French Silversmith Company Inspired by Corrugated Cardboard

Whiteread said she also agreed to design the statue in an effort to safeguard arts and culture, which she described as being “under very real threat.” “The Brits have celebrated musical creativity and artistry for decades now. We have some fantastically creative musicians who have produced music that lays their souls bare, provides hope in times of darkness, or speaks directly about a moment in time,” she added.

In designing the trophy, Whiteread joins a prestigious list of other artists who have given the statue new life: Dame Peter Blake, Tracey Emin, Vivienne Westwood and Yinka Ilori. In 1997, Whiteread became the first woman to represent Britain at the Venice Biennale, and in 2001, she became the third artist to have her work placed on the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, which took the form of an inverted resin recreation of the plinth.

#9020. Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum

A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro.

While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media. Related Articles British Museums Are Experiencing a 'Bayeux Bounce' in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry Scientists Say They've Rediscovered How the Romans Made the British Museum's Color-Shifting Lycurgus Cup

ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.

The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

There are discounts on other capacities too.UK deal: £477.89 £370.49 at Amazon UK

#9018. rounded volumes and sweet color palettes shape dessert-inspired lighting collection

what if a lamp could be as tempting as your favorite dessert? decadent studio presents chubby, a collection of table lamps inspired by the shapes, colors and textures of sweet treats.

decadentstudio edited by christina vergopoulou November 27, 2026 2 min

Chubby is the first lighting collection by Decadent Studio, an independent design studio based in Galicia, Spain. Inspired by desserts such as pavlova, cherry pie and tangerine ice cream, the collection explores the relationship between food, design and desire. The lamp is defined by its rounded shapes, generous proportions and soft curves. Each color is inspired by a different dessert, which also gives the lamp its name. When switched off, Chubby is a sculptural object. When lit, its colors take on a different character, creating a soft, warm glow.

Each lamp is made to order in Galicia using a recyclable, plant-based biopolymer, avoiding unnecessary stock and overproduction. Every piece is individually numbered and comes with its own certificate of authenticity. Decadent Studio pays special attention to every detail, from the color of the textile cable to the back of the lamp. Chubby is designed to be seen from every angle. Behind the collection is a simple idea: designing objects that bring us pleasure, just as our favourite desserts do. Objects of desire. Guilt-free pleasures.

#9017. German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth

We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes. Related Articles Museum Wiesbaden Will Be Germany's First Institution to Return Colonial-Era Human Remains to Indonesia The Netherlands and Germany Agree to Return 2,000 Artifacts to Ghana

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

#9016. "Europe's largest museum development" opens in 1930s Citroën garage in Brussels

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

Brussels‘ former Citroën Garage has been transformed into Kanal, a 40,000-square-metre museum for modern art and architecture with an exhibition programme developed with the Parisian art institution Centre Pompidou.

The transformation was designed by Atelier Kanal, a consortium made up of architecture studio EM2N, NoAarchitecten and Sergison Bates Architects, with a team of construction workers, who restored the 1930s industrial building and added three new volumes within its structure.

Claiming to be “Europe’s largest museum development”, Kanal – sometimes referred to as Kanal-Centre Pompidou – hopes to provide space for people to gather to enjoy visual art, performance, dance, music, film and architecture.

Opening to the public on 28 November, the canal-side building was originally built in 1934 as a garage and showroom for the car company Citroën.

Atelier Kanal aimed to keep the industrial character of the building by implementing a “light touch” approach, restoring most of the building fabric, repairing and upgrading parts where needed, and replacing other parts to improve climatic and acoustic conditions.

The garage’s former showroom, a modernist curved glass building with 20-metre-tall interiors, was converted into a gallery space topped with a publicly accessible rooftop.

“Rather than a spectacular gesture, our proposal offers an attitude of ‘radical optimism’ – open and non-prescriptive, spontaneous and instinctive – much like the spirit of modern progress in which it was created,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The interior is a fine example of elegant industrial engineering, while the glass facades clearly express early modernism,” it continued.

“Our ambition has been to trust the building as we found it, embracing its industrial character and many layers of use.”

Three new buildings were added inside the existing structure, including a four-storey volume with a basement level that contains art galleries, and another volume housing a 378-seat auditorium and the Kanal offices.

The third volume is the new home for Brussels’ museum and archive of architecture, Kanal Architecture, which was formerly known as CIVA.

Rising nine stories on the north-east side of the campus, across from the art galleries, the structure includes exhibition spaces, a library, archives, research centre, bookshop and workshop spaces.

Architecture collective Assemble designed an indoor playground on the first floor of the museum, which features playscapes informed by volcanoes, planets, and piles of coal that were once transported on the canal.

Elsewhere in the building are a library, bookshop, rooftop bar, restaurants and an in-house bakery.

Kanal’s year-round programme of exhibitions was developed in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou art museum in Paris.

“Kanal invites citizens, organisations, collectives and communities to appropriate and inhabit large parts of the building, for production, performances, events, informal gatherings or simply to spend time,” said Atelier Kanal.

“The museum extends beyond curated art, becoming part of the city and its fabric,” it continued. “In this sense, Kanal departs from the traditional museum and instead offers a place for civic gathering, responding to the growing absence of shared public spaces in our cities today.”

Other museums that have recently opened in historic buildings include the London Museum, located in a transformed Victorian market building, and a bank in Santander that was transformed into the Faro Santander museum.

Photography by Koen Van Damme unless otherwise stated. Video by Eyes–Screen.

#9014. Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History

All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022. Related Articles EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale Russian Teenager Detained After Posting Neo-Nazi Threats on TikTok, Targeting Moscow Museum

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

#9013. 1960s grand touring car design shapes acte deux’s paris apartment renovation

inspired by automotive interiors and streamlined bodywork, the 65-square-meter renovation combines lacquered surfaces, polished metal and warm timber to rethink domestic space.

Acte Deux, founded by Johanna Lapray and Hugo L’ahélec, renovates a 65-square-meter apartment in the Paris’s 18th arrondissement, drawing on the streamlined forms and richly appointed interiors of 1960s grand touring cars. Named Gran Turismo, the project takes its reference from an era of automotive design associated with sculptural bodywork, polished details and comfortable interiors, translating these qualities into a domestic setting.

Located on the 10th floor of a 1960s concrete residential building, the apartment originally had standard ceiling heights and relatively constrained volumes. Rather than working against these limitations, the designers reorganize the interior around its expansive views of the French capital and the rooftops surrounding Sacré-Cœur.

Paris-based design studio Acte Deux reorganizes the living spaces into a continuous horizontal sequence. Living and dining areas extend along the main facade, where a large bay window and five additional windows frame the city panorama. The open layout makes the most of the views across Paris, bringing the surrounding city into the living spaces. A palette of natural whites, creams, browns and oak establishes a relatively restrained foundation. Against it, saturated lacquered surfaces in garnet, orange and blue introduce the more expressive language of the Gran Turismo reference. Warm, understated materials provide continuity, while glossy finishes bring movement and visual punctuation to the space.

One of the clearest references appears at floor level. An orange lacquered ribbon runs around the oak parquet, framing the floor like the pinstripe detailing found along the bodywork of vintage touring cars. The parquet itself recalls the original mosaic flooring, retaining a connection to the existing character of the apartment.

Across the living room wall, two sheets of polished chrome-like metal extend horizontally, recalling the appearance of an automotive radiator grille. In the dining area, a glossy blue lacquered table adds another concentrated burst of color, vintage chairs and a painting by Hervé Priou bring contrasting textures and references into the composition.

In the kitchen, Acte Deux pairs a matte lacquered kitchen with a Travertino Rosso worktop and a curved beige cabinet with glass portholes separates the kitchen from the adjoining spaces. Its rounded profile softens the transition between rooms, introducing a sculptural element that echoes the aerodynamic forms behind the project’s automotive inspiration.

The bathroom develops this language through a combination of stained and varnished wood, bronzed wall lacquer and black-and-white checkerboard porcelain stoneware tiles. The pattern evokes racing flags, extending the Gran Turismo narrative into a more intimate part of the apartment.

An orange corridor connects the main living area to the bedroom, creating a colorful passage between the public and private zones of the apartment. A concealed door opens the perspective toward the opposite end of the interior, revealing the cross-ventilated configuration of the house. Beyond a dressing area screened by wool curtains with green edging, the bedroom features thick carpeting, warm materials and a desk facing the park.

Across the renovation, Acte Deux uses references from automotive design as a framework for organizing a domestic environment. The project moves between the precision of industrial detailing and the familiarity of residential materials, combining polished metal, lacquer, timber and stone into a sequence of distinct but connected spaces.

#9012. Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale, Report Details Limited Damage to Bayeux Tapestry Following Transport to the British Museum, and More: Morning Links for November 27, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

THE PRINCESS AND THE VENICE BIENNALE. Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s largest recurring art exhibition, which runs from April 8 to November 26, 2028, ARTnews reports. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority. She will be the first Arab curator of the Venice Biennale, and was selected upon the recommendation of its president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. In a statement, Al Qasimi said: “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco and the board for their confidence and trust.” Related Articles Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion Honored in 2026 Venice Biennale Awards, Smithsonian Secretary Responds to Leaked Plans, Marianne Boesky to Open Paris Gallery, and More: Morning Links for November 25, 2026 South African Artist Tamlin Blake Found Dead, Germany to Restitute Archive of Nazi-Persecuted Jehovah's Witnesses to Family, and More: Morning Links for November 24, 2026

DAMAGE REPORT. A report made public yesterday by France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, Le Figaro reports. While the overall state of the 950-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened before the voyage. The loan of the fragile tapestry was heavily criticized for risking damage to the artifact, but was ultimately made possible in part thanks to carefully controlled ground transport that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations. The artifact has since become the hottest museum show in London, attracting long lines and selling out tickets within minutes.

A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for £1.5 million ($1.97 million), and it is among several rediscovered paintings in an exhibition titled Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, open until December 18. [The Art Newspaper]

Two illuminated manuscripts and three crosses from the 15th century were returned from the American collection of Robert McCarthy to Ethiopia, as part of a unique new partnership between the Ethiopian Heritage Authority (EHA), the Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) and McCarthy. [The Voice]

Veruschka, the German supermodel, who became an iconic muse to the fashion, arts and cultural world of the 1960s and 70s, has died at 87. [WWD]

Neil Simmons, a sculptor whose famous marble piece depicting Margaret Thatcher was decapitated by a protester, has died at 73. [The Times of London]

A rare “Breast Bowl,” or “jatte-téton,” that belonged to French Queen Marie Antoinette and was used in her royal “pleasure dairy,” hammered in Paris for $3.23 million with fees, beating its high estimate of $2.19 million. [ARTnews]

The Princess of Wales, spent time at the Hugo Burge Foundation in Berwickshire, which supports the arts in the UK, and she spoke about the healing qualities of art-making with painter Siobhan McLaughlin, who makes her own pigment and works with stone and earth. [Times of London]

KANALIZING. On Saturday, Kanal or Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels’ nearly 10-acre “city-museum,” opens to the public, heralding the Belgian capital’s first major modern and contemporary art museum organized in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou. As ARTnews reported in September, the mega-project of free and ticketed spaces has been met with controversy over the course of its decade in the making, notably because of ongoing uncertainty about its financial survival, its cost, as well as its dependence on the Pompidou in Paris. Unless there is a political turnabout, Kanal’s publicly funded budget allocated by the Brussels-Capital Region is expected to drop from its current €28 million to €10 million by 2029, which is not enough to keep the project running, according to its leaders. This week, at a large press conference attended by ARTnews, Boris Dilliès, the minister-president of the Brussels region, was on the defensive about the initiative, he said he has faith, while admitting to heavy criticism. The story of Kanal’s rocky road to becoming reality has been widely reported in stories pegged to this week’s opening, but few have offered their thoughts on the 10 exhibitions debuting with it, and what it’s like to wander the vast halls of this new cultural phenomenon. ARTnews stayed on to more fully experience the myriad of shows open to previewing guests, which, over the course of two days, included artists and about 5,000 local schoolchildren. Watch this space to hear our take on Europe’s latest, highly ambitious cultural endeavor, including where it already shines, and where there is room – literally, a whole lot of space – for much more still to come.

#9010. Keira Knightley’s Emerald-Green ‘Atonement’ Gown Heads to Christie’s

The stunning emerald-green plunging-back gown worn by actress Keira Knightley in Atonement will be auctioned live in London on December 9 at Christie’s. It is estimated to fetch between £100,000 and £120,000 ($130,940 to $157,125). In addition, the sale titled Love & Lust: A Literary Guide, will offer a host of items “celebrating the many expressions of love, romance and desire,” per the auction house’s description. This will range from passionate letters and cinematic costumes behind famous romances played out on stage and in literature, including about 30 books, manuscripts, autographed letters and original works dating back centuries. Related Articles Christie's Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio Yoshitomo Nara Painting Fetches $15.9 M., Outselling Koons and Richter in New York

Knightley wore the silky green ensemble designed by Jacqueline Durran for her role as Cecilia Tallis in the 2007 film Atonement, adapted from Ian McEwan’s acclaimed novel, and directed by Joe Wright. The dress last went under the hammer in a charity auction in 2008 and fetched £35,000 ($46,000).

Also for sale are rare examples of early film poster art, including one of the influential film Metropolis, made in 1926 for its premiere, estimated at £100,000 to £130,000 ($130,940 to $170,220). Another poster for Dracula (1931), which marked a pivotal moment for early sound movies, is being offered for an estimated £80,000 to £120,000 ($104,750 to $157,125).

These lots are joined, among others, by early 19th-century love letters from the celebrated British Royal Navy officer Horatio Nelson to Emma, Lady Hamilton, estimated at £5,000 and £8,000, plus original sketches by Chris Foss for the publication of The Joy of Sex (1972), estimated at £6,000 to £8,000.

“Love and desire have inspired some of the most enduring stories in literature and art, and this sale brings together a wonderfully eclectic group of objects that capture their many facets…” jointly stated Thais Hitchins, associate specialist, and Mark Wiltshire, specialist, Christie’s London.

#9009. singapore’s artscience museum shows design beyond the human realm

discover how design goes beyond humans to include animals and ecosystems as active collaborators in this expanded exhibition

When the Design Museum, London developed More than Human: Making With the Living World, it began with a deceptively simple proposition: what if design were not understood as solely by and for humans, but as something shaped in collaboration with animals, plants, and ecosystems?

Living environments are already shaped by countless organisms and relationships, each participating in the ecosystems of which humans are also a part. The exhibition asks how design might acknowledge these relationships, shifting away from an understanding of nature as a resource toward ways of craft that recognize other living beings as participants and collaborators. Ultimately, it invites us to develop more reciprocal and responsible relationships with the living world.

Following its presentation in Zurich, the exhibition now makes it way to Singapore. From November 28, 2026, to May 16, 2027, visitors can experience More than Human: Making With the Living World at ArtScience Museum.

Building on the original London presentation, the Singapore edition has been significantly expanded and co-curated by ArtScience Museum and the Design Museum, London, with support from the DesignSingapore Council.

Twenty-four works and installations by regional artists, including commissions, adaptations, and international loans, join the existing exhibition. This brings the total to more than 140 artworks, objects, and installations contributed by close to 55 artists, designers, architects, researchers, and communities, notably featuring the works of eight local Singaporean designers.

The additions bring perspectives from across Southeast Asia into the exhibition, exploring how design can be understood as part of living, interconnected systems rather than as something separate from the living world.

The exhibition includes basketry by Ye’kuana people from the Amazon region, whose practices reflect relationships between material gathering, cultural knowledge, and the forest.

There is also Aki Inomata’s How to carve a sculpture. Inomata placed wooden blocks in beaver enclosures and collected the forms left by their gnawing. Because beavers tend to chew around hard knots, the wood itself helps shape what emerges. She presents the beaver-gnawed originals alongside two versions enlarged to three times their size: one hand-carved by a sculptor, the other produced using computer-controlled milling (CNC). By placing all three side by side, Inomata asks who, or what, creates a sculpture: the beaver, the wood, the sculptor, the machine, the artist, or the relationships among them?

Taking a more hands-on but equally reflective approach, MOTH’s The More-than-human Rights mural explores Rights of Nature frameworks, exploring a world where rivers and ecosystems are recognized as living entities with intrinsic rights. Masks available to visitors reveal texts hidden in the mural.

Also worth highlighting is Zheng Mahler’s Lantau Trilogy, presented in full in this format for the first time, which focuses on the non-human inhabitants of Hong Kong’s Lantau Island. It unfolds in three acts, each devoted to a different inhabitant: bats, water buffaloes, and fungi.

To help visitors immerse themselves in these ideas, Lekker Architects designed an exhibition space that encourages shifting perspectives. Drawing abstract inspiration from navigating a hedge maze, the formation of archipelagos, and wandering through woodlands, the spatial design invites visitors to encounter the living world from different viewpoints and reconsider their place within it.

More than Human: Making With the Living World will be on view at ArtScience Museum until May 2027.

exhibition: More than Human: Making With the Living World

#9008. Are GLP-1 Drugs Quietly Changing Our Sex Lives?

By now you’ve probably heard about GLP-1s, sold under brand names such as Ozempic and Wegovy. This class of medications mimics naturally occurring hormones involved in appetite control and blood sugar regulation to treat type 2 diabetes and aid weight-loss efforts. It should be no surprise, then, that conversations around these popular drugs have largely centered on the scale. However, some scientists are starting to look more closely into how they may impact something perhaps even more personal: our sex lives.

At present roughly one in five Americans reports taking or having taken a GLP-1, according to a recent poll. As the number of people using these medications has soared, so have anecdotal reports about how they’re impacting users’ day-to-day—and yes, this includes things like pleasure and sex drive. Though there hasn’t been a ton of research into the relationship between sexual health and GLP-1s yet, more scientists are starting to investigate potential impacts.

In a review published in Obesity Pillars in March 2026, for example, researchers propose that GLP-1s may influence desire by impacting brain chemistry. But how exactly might these drugs impact sex drive? And is there a way to remain engaged in your sex life while on a GLP-1? We tapped experts to find out.

To understand how GLP-1s might influence libido, it helps to walk through how they work more broadly.

Some options, like Wegovy and Ozempic, contain semaglutide, which is a synthetic version of a naturally occurring hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1, or GLP-1. Semaglutide binds to GLP-1 receptors throughout the brain and body, helping regulate appetite, blood sugar, and feelings of satiety, James Simon, MD, an ob-gyn and reproductive endocrinologist and one of the researchers behind the Obesity Pillars study, tells SELF.

Other options, like Zepbound and Mounjaro, contain a different active ingredient called tirzepatide, which mimics both GLP-1 and a related hormone, and thus impacts the body in similar ways to semaglutide.

On top of reporting reduced appetite and increased satiety, a number of patients have also found that these weight-loss medications quiet what they call “food noise.” But as it turns out, the same parts of the brain that control appetite are also responsible for other reward-seeking behaviors, according to Dr. Simon. He says this could help explain why taking GLP-1s may have the auxiliary impact of decreasing appetite for another pleasurable activity: sex.

On top of that, early research suggests that GLP-1s may affect certain serotonin receptors, including one called 5-HT2C. This is thought to be a key player in the sexual side effects often experienced by those taking selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), such as reduced libido and delayed orgasm.

“We know that, while SSRIs are fantastic options for anxiety and depression, they can have a significant impact on sexual desire and orgasmic function in both men and women,” says Dr. Simon. “It makes sense that other medications that also impact serotonin pathways might have similar impacts on sexual desire in some individuals.”

Sexual function isn’t just about hormones and brain chemistry. It also depends on the pelvic floor, a group of muscles that support the bladder and bowel, among other organs, and play an active role in arousal and orgasm, explains pelvic-health physical therapist Iris Xu, PT, DPT, of Fusion Wellness & Femina Physical Therapy.

“During arousal the pelvic-floor muscles increase blood flow to the genitals,” Dr. Xu says. During penetration the muscles lengthen and relax to allow for comfortable insertion and boost sensation. And during orgasm they contract rhythmically, creating the pulsing feeling associated with climax, she says.

In general, weight loss—from GLP-1s or other methods—can improve pelvic-floor function because reduced abdominal pressure means the muscles don’t have to work as hard to support the pelvic organs, Dr. Xu says. A 2024 study published in Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics found that women carrying more fat, particularly in the pelvic area, had weaker pelvic floor muscles than those with less.

But GLP-1s don’t just encourage fat loss. Because these medications can lead to relatively rapid weight loss, preserving lean muscle mass can be challenging—especially without adequate protein intake or resistance training, says Dr. Xu. “[GLP-1s] can also cause loss of lean body mass and strength, especially when used in isolation without exercise or diet modifications,” she adds. In extreme cases this can lead to a condition called sarcopenia, which some studies have linked to reduced pelvic floor function. (FWIW, muscle loss can occur no matter how you lose weight. But by accelerating the weight-loss process, GLP-1s may speed up muscle loss as well.)

At the time of writing, research specifically examining GLP-1 medications and pelvic-floor outcomes remains limited. There is also little data on these drugs’ impact on muscle loss. But the research we do have points to this being a likely outcome, and Dr. Xu says losing too much lean mass may weaken pelvic floor support. This, in turn, can affect arousal, orgasm intensity, or overall sexual function.

As mentioned earlier, part of the notoriety of these medications is the speed at which many patients lose weight. Research has shown that, on average, people who are overweight or living with obesity can lose anywhere from roughly 10% to 20% of their total body weight on a GLP-1, depending on factors like which drug they use, what dose they take, and how long they continue treatment.

However, despite cultural messages to the contrary, weight loss does not automatically translate to increased body confidence and desire, Joy Berkheimer, PhD, LMFT, a sex and relationship therapist, tells SELF.

“Particularly if you have a long history of having your body policed against external beauty standards—as most women and people assigned female at birth do—the rapidity of the physical changes can lead you to feel unfamiliar in your body,” she says. Sexual desire and pleasure are often closely tied to embodiment, so a lack of embodiment can impact intimacy, she says.

It’s not all bad news; for some people the broader health changes associated with these drugs may actually improve aspects of sexual well-being. People go on GLP-1s for help with a variety of health conditions, such as obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), to name just a few. Addressing these sorts of underlying issues may benefit sexual health.

That means even if the medications dial down some of the brain signals tied to desire, other changes happening in the body (e.g., improved energy, hormone balance, and physical comfort) may help support a healthier sex life, Dr. Simon tells SELF.

“Fat cells are highly inflammatory and impede our well-being far beyond their impact on our weight, leading to things such as joint pain and muscle fatigue,” he says. Feeling weak and achy can reduce interest in any physical activity—sex included!—as well as decrease pleasure during them. But as fat mass decreases and inflammation drops, people may feel more comfortable, energetic, and ultimately sexier. Additionally, as body composition improves, hormone levels may shift in ways that boost sexual desire and function, particularly in those with dysfunction, Dr. Simon says. (Body fat contains enzymes that can convert testosterone into estrogen. When levels of these hormones are unbalanced, it can impact sexual health.)

GLP-1 medications have also been shown to improve markers associated with vascular health, including blood pressure. Healthy blood flow is essential to arousal in people of all genders, says Dr. Simon. For those with vaginas it supports clitoral engorgement, lubrication, and vaginal expansion.

Finally, as metabolic health improves some people will see an increase in their energy levels and feel more comfortable in their bodies, says board-certified bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist Betsy Dovec, MD, FACS, DBOM. For some—particularly those navigating postpartum body changes or the menopause transition—that renewed energy and groundedness can translate into increased confidence and desire, she says.

Taken altogether these physiological shifts can enhance sexual function for some people, even as the medications potentially continue to lower the volume on certain reward pathways.

Of course, our sex lives aren’t driven by biology alone. They are mediated by culture and society, the relationships we’re in, our sense of self and self-confidence, and more. The broader life changes that can accompany weight loss may shift libido north or south.

In a society that often equates thinness with desirability, people who don’t fall into the narrow confines of “thin” may feel undesirable, unsexy, or even undeserving of pleasure. For some individuals changes in body composition toward that supposed ideal may lead to increased confidence.

A 2025 survey from the Kinsey Institute and DatingAdvice.com found that 59% of GLP-1 agonist users said the medication had an impact on their dating life, with a number saying it boosted their confidence. Justin Lehmiller, PhD, a social psychologist, research fellow at the Kinsey Institute, and host of the Sex and Psychology podcast, tells SELF that confidence can have huge impacts on our sexual satisfaction.

“Feeling confident makes it easier to surrender to pleasure and facilitates communicating about our sexual needs and desires, which helps to ensure that we’re getting more of what we want in bed,” he says. “By contrast, when we aren’t feeling confident, it’s easy to get stuck in our heads during intimacy and start worrying about things like how we look.”

For those who are single, increased self-confidence may inspire someone who previously didn’t use dating apps or go out to bars because of body image hang-ups to start putting themselves in situations where connection feels more possible, Dr. Simon says. Meanwhile, in long-term relationships that confidence could translate into greater willingness to initiate sex or say yes to a partner’s advances, he adds. It may also mean someone feels more comfortable experimenting with positions they once shied away from—potentially even discovering ones that bring them more pleasure.

In these cases the reward pathways are still muted. However, because other things that shape sexual desire and enjoyment (like confidence) have increased, patients on these drugs may be experiencing better and/or more sex overall.

“Changes in libido are among the most common concerns people bring into sex therapy,” Dr. Berkheimer says. “But often they are a completely normal response to life transitions or physiological shifts, rather than a sign that something is wrong.”

Desire isn’t static, she explains. Rather, it fluctuates across the lifespan in response to factors like stress, sleep quality, exercise routine, medication, illness, hormones, relationship dynamics, and more. That means any shifts you notice after starting a GLP-1 medication aren’t necessarily a sign that something is off—your body might just need time to adjust, Dr. Berkheimer says. Still, if the change feels distressing or different enough to affect your well-being or relationships, it’s worth bringing up with your doctor.

Sexual health, Dr. Dovec says, isn’t a frivolous concern. “Pleasure matters. Intimacy matters. Feeling sexy matters. These are at the core of quality of life,” she says. Shifts in sexual desire and function can offer useful information about what’s happening in your body more broadly. So if sexual changes happen, talk to your provider. As frustrating or unwelcome as these shifts can be, they’re often temporary or solvable with a provider’s help, according to Dr. Dovec.

Sometimes the solution is as simple as adjusting GLP-1 dosage or timing; other times a clinician may suggest lifestyle changes, like adjusting your diet or exercise routine, or additional treatments that support hormone balance.

Not sure how to start the conversation? Dr. Dovec suggests keeping it simple: “You can just say, ‘Something feels different,’ or ‘I don’t feel like myself sexually.’ You’re not going to shock or embarrass your doctor.”

If you find yourself missing pleasure during this season of libidinal lull, Dr. Berkheimer encourages approaching your body with curiosity rather than pressure and expanding intimacy beyond intercourse. “That can look like slowing down and focusing on sensation instead of performance, exploring non-goal-oriented touch like massage or extended skin-to-skin contact, [or experimenting with] sex toys or pleasure aids,” she tells SELF.

Working with a body-neutral or Health at Every Size (HAES) sex therapist can also help you navigate medication effects, physical changes, identity, cultural conditioning, and more so you can erect an updated pleasure practice that honors the body you’re in now, Dr. Berkheimer adds.

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#9006. Base Design gives Visa a brand refresh "for the next generation"

Design agency Base Design has created a more compact version of credit card company Visa’s logo and worked with Displaay Type Foundry on a new typeface, as part of a refresh of the brand’s visual identity.

While the 2021 Visa wordmark remains unchanged, the refresh included creating a shortened symbol for the brand, rolling out the new Visa Sans typeface, and creating a blocky hero graphic to market towards a younger generation.

“When you’re working with a brand as iconic as Visa, the challenge isn’t recognition – it’s relevance,” said Base Design executive creative director Min Lew.

“Our ambition was to build on Visa’s extraordinary equity while giving it a renewed sense of energy and expression, one that feels as relevant to the next generation as it does to the generations who have grown up with it.”

As part of this strategy, the studio cut the V out of the existing wordmark to function as its own symbol. It will be used on credit cards and appear across digital platforms.

The studio also wrapped it in colourful bar, which will also be used on graphic elements such as posters, and to frame text.

“More than a framing device, the hero graphic device brings movement, direction, and possibility to the identity,” said Lew.

“This simple gesture becomes the foundation for a visual language that can be energetic at a global sporting event, confident and bold in a B2B environment, or vibrant and elevated for affluent audiences.”

For Visa Sans, Base Design and Displaay Type Foundry also based the design on the existing logo.

The typeface features rounded edges akin to the rounded corner of the Visa V, and overall, extends “the logo’s character across the wider identity”.

Ultimately, the new identity was created to be used across different smaller, touchpoints according to the team, such as at tap-to-pay stations, at checkout, or online, as the brand appears “for only a moment” in day to day life.

“We have deep trust and recognition as a brand,” said Visa chief marketing officer Frank Cooper III. “This refresh gives us an opportunity to build on that.”

A more subtle approach to logo and branding updates has been popular in recent years, such as at Walmart and Google.

In contrast, the US restaurant chain Cracker Barrel recently took a hard swing at a logo update, which was immediately met with online backlash and promptly scrapped in favour of the original design.

#9005. a review of midcentury kinetic environments: when artists turned entire rooms into moving machines

in the 1960s, artists began using motors, elastic structures, and pneumatic systems to transform the spaces we inhabit.

Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, an international network of artists began to explore the possibilities of kinetic art at the scale of architecture. Motors and electrical circuits found their way into museum galleries, where entire interiors could be animated with moving structures and artificial light. In some cases, the machinery responded to the viewer’s presence.

An early precedent for these experiments came from the Bauhaus. In 1930, Hungarian artist László Moholy-Nagy introduced his Light Prop for an Electric Stage, also known as the Light-Space Modulator, at an exhibition in Paris. As the machine’s metal components rotated, light passed through perforated surfaces and bounced off reflective elements. Its movements generated a second composition across the surrounding walls. Here was a sculpture whose physical dimensions accounted for only a fraction of the space it occupied.

By the time Galerie Denise René staged its landmark exhibition Le Mouvement in Paris in 1955, movement had become the subject of a budding international art movement. Artists were experimenting with industrial technologies at a moment of renewed interest in the relationship between art and engineering. Over the following decade, some of the most ambitious projects in kinetic art would take the form of environments that visitors could physically enter.

László Moholy-Nagy, Light Prop for an Electric Stage (Light-Space Modulator) | video courtesy SFMOMA

In 1961, a 52-meter steel tower by Franco-Hungarian artist Nicolas Schöffer rose beside the Palais des Congrès in Liège, Belgium. An arrangement of rotating reflective panels occupied its open framework, while an electronic control system coordinated its movements with light and sound. Schöffer also developed an animated light wall for the neighboring building. After dark, the project extended across the riverfront as reflections appeared on the surface of the Meuse.

Schöffer had been studying cybernetics, a field concerned with systems of communication and feedback. His earlier robotic sculpture, CYSP 1 (1956), incorporated sensors through which it could respond to changes in its surroundings. With the Liège project, the artist could begin to imagine how these relationships between machines and their environments might operate at an urban scale.

At the third Paris Biennale in 1963, the Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) constructed a labyrinth of its own. The collective, whose members included Julio Le Parc and François Morellet, assembled a series of experiments with light and physical movement. Visitors encountered works that required their participation. GRAV would eventually take these experiments beyond the museum and onto the streets of Paris in 1966.

For Documenta III in Kassel in 1964, the German artists Heinz Mack, Otto Piene, and Günther Uecker of the ZERO group collaborated on Light Room (Homage to Fontana). In the darkened gallery, seven kinetic sculptures and a projected image formed a single installation. Electric motors and timers governed the activity of its individual components. As reflective surfaces turned and the distribution of light changed, the room took on a rhythm of its own.

The work built upon experiments that Piene had begun in the late 1950s with his Lichtballett (Light Ballets). The artist initially manipulated light sources by hand, before developing motorized devices that could perform their own sequences. For ZERO, the ephemeral qualities of light offered a way to work at an architectural scale without the construction of a permanent structure.

What might be one of the most compelling environments of the period emerged from the Italian artist Gianni Colombo‘s research into spatial perception. A co-founder of Milan’s Gruppo T in 1959, Colombo had developed a series of kinetic works before turning his attention to installations large enough to accommodate the human body.

At the 1967 Trigon exhibition in Graz, Austria, he presented Spazio elastico (Elastic Space), a darkened interior filled with a three-dimensional network of elastic cords. Under ultraviolet light, the cords appeared as luminous lines suspended in space. Two motors occasionally stretched the grid out of shape, so that the seemingly regular arrangement of cubes gradually lost its symmetry.

There’s something especially architectural about Colombo’s approach. With very few materials, he could manipulate the perceived proportions of an interior and interfere with the body’s sense of orientation. The familiar logic of an orthogonal space gave way to a geometry that shifted as visitors navigated it. In 1968, the work earned the artist first prize in painting at the Venice Biennale.

In Vienna, the experiments of the Austrian avant-garde collective Haus-Rucker-Co brought a new dimension to kinetic environments through the use of inflatable architecture. Founded in 1967 by architects Laurids Ortner and Günter Zamp Kelp alongside artist Klaus Pinter, the group explored how unconventional architectural forms could alter the sensory experiences of their inhabitants.

Their 1968 project Gelbes Herz (Yellow Heart) took the form of a pneumatic capsule just large enough for two people. Occupants entered through a series of inflatable rings before settling onto a transparent plastic mattress inside a spherical chamber. The surrounding air-filled cushions periodically swelled toward their bodies and receded, so that the interior seemed to breathe around them.

Across the translucent membranes, brightly colored dots shifted in appearance as the plastic expanded and contracted. Haus-Rucker-Co had effectively designed a room with its own pulse. The project belonged to a wider body of architectural experiments in which lightweight synthetic materials and air pressure offered alternatives to the rigidity of conventional construction.

By 1970, many of these ideas had found their way into a single building at the World Exposition in Osaka, Japan. The Pepsi Pavilion was developed by Experiments in Art and Technology (E.A.T.), an organization that grew out of collaborations between artists and engineers in New York. Its members transformed a faceted dome into an environment whose appearance could change from one moment to the next.

Outside the pavilion, Japanese artist Fujiko Nakaya enveloped the architecture in a cloud of artificially generated fog. The density and shape of the cloud varied with atmospheric conditions. Across the plaza, a collection of white, motorized sculptures by American artist Robert Breer traveled so slowly that their movements became apparent over time.

Inside the building, visitors entered a vast mirrored chamber around ninety feet in diameter. Its curved reflective surface produced inverted images of the people below, who appeared to float in the air above their own heads. Laser light and a spatial sound system introduced further variables into the interior. The pavilion’s architecture could be experienced differently according to the weather outside, the electronic activity within, and the position of each visitor.

#9004. Royal Society for Arts appoints five Royal Designers for Industry

The UK’s Royal Society for Arts has announced five Royal Designers for Industry, who include Durrell Bishop and Bridget Baines, as well as naming an Honorary Royal Designer as it celebrates its 90th anniversary.

The awards, which were established in 1936, recognise outstanding talent across landscape architecture, technology, illustration, fashion and theatre. They are given by Royal Society for Arts (RSA) and can only be held by 200 designers at any one time.

This year’s winners are product and interaction designer Bishop, multidisciplinary designer Harris Elliott, illustrator Laura Carlin, costume designer Tahra Zafar and landscape architect Bridget Baines.

Baines co-founded international practice Gross Max, and her fellow Gross Max founder Eelco Hooftman (pictured in main image with Baines) was given the Honorary Royal Designer award this year.

The winners were chosen for their “joyful” designs,

“Ninety years on, the Royal Designers are still looking forward,” Keeper of the Faculty of Royal Designers for Industry Johanna Gibbons said. “This year’s appointments show how far design now reaches, from public landscapes and picture books to exhibitions, the stage and the objects we use every day.”

“Their work is joyful, and it is serious about making life better,” she continued. “That is what unites Royal Designers across the decades: a living entanglement of disciplines that, with the RSA Fellowship, is a profound force for good.”

Last year’s winners included designer Yinka Ilori and journalist Mona Chalabi, and the award has also been given to designers including Es Devlin, Vivienne Westwood, James Dyson and Zandra Rhodes.

According to the RSA, the winners represent the “sheer breadth of design today”.

“Great design changes how we experience the world, often in ways we barely notice,” RSA programme manager Catherine Joyce.

“For 90 years, Royal Designers have shown what extraordinary creativity can achieve, and how it can make life better for everyone,” she continued.“These six appointments are a wonderful reminder of the sheer breadth of design today.”

Dezeen also recently celebrated the best designers of this year as part of our Dezeen Awards, including Ilori, Yasmine Ghoniem and Keiji Ashizawa.
